Chapter 6: The Machinery of the State and the Illusion of Neutrality
Picture this: most of us grow up thinking that the rules and institutions running our society are like the referees in a game—impartial, fair, and just there to keep things running smoothly.
But if you've ever spent time trying to actually get help from the system, you know it doesn’t always feel that way.
Imagine a tenant, dealing with unsafe living conditions, who tries to file a complaint. All they get is a mountain of paperwork, and every time they think they’ve done what’s asked, the requirements seem to change.
Or think about a worker who’s passionate about organizing a union, hoping for a fair shot—only to find the law seems to throw up barriers at every turn.
In moments like these, the state doesn’t feel neutral at all. It feels like a fortress—one built to protect some people and keep others on the outside.
Most folks don’t notice this at first. The courts, the police, the politicians—they all talk about fairness and order. But as time goes on, patterns start to stand out.
The same neighborhoods get policed more harshly. The same voices get ignored at city council meetings. And, somehow, the same big corporations keep winning contracts, no matter who holds office.
It starts to become clear: the machinery of the state isn’t just a bunch of tools lying around—it’s a system, carefully designed to keep things the way they are.
If you’re hoping for change, that realization can hit hard.
Reformers often believe that by winning elections or passing new laws, they’ll finally get the state to work for the people. But the more they push, the more they see how the system pushes back.
Politicians make big promises, but then loopholes appear. New laws are celebrated, but suddenly, no one’s enforcing them. The state isn’t a blank slate—it’s got its own interests, its own way of protecting those who already have power.
Now, that doesn’t mean change is impossible. Small victories can and do happen. And sometimes, they make a real difference.
But the idea that the state is just a neutral stage for progress? That fades away.
The state isn’t above the struggle—it’s part of it.
So, what does that mean for anyone who dreams of a different world?
It means the fight for change isn’t just about rewriting the rules. It’s about challenging the very institutions that enforce them.
Picture our tenant, walking out of that government office. They’re frustrated, maybe even angry, but underneath that, there’s a new kind of determination.
The path ahead is tougher than they expected, but the lesson is clear: real change means more than just new laws. It means building new forms of power—sometimes outside, and sometimes even against, the old machinery.
